# Introduction

One thing I have heard many times is that Bayesian methods have no mechanism to control false positives, while Frequentist methods just allow you to apply a p-value correction (e.g. Bonferroni) to control your false positive rate.

The typical Bayesian response is that this concern misunderstands the theory behind Bayesian statistics (In Bayesland, probability is "degree of belief" while in Frequentistland probability is the frequency of a given event over repeated trials). Which is true, but not helpful.

So instead, let's actually talk about why this matters. It's a fair concern from the Frequentist camp that if you go full-Bayes you risk being over-enthusiastic about your data. So what can be done about it?

## Skeptical Priors

Scientists are meant to be skeptical. If you've ever been to a seminar when some of the cranky faculty are around, you know what I'm talking about.

To appease these scientists, you can present your results with a "skeptical prior." This is one that assumes whatever effect you're looking for will be very small, and biases you against finding a result. 

Let me demonstrate with a concrete example.

```{python}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
import scipy.stats as stats
import scipy.special as special

plt.style.use("bmh")
```

# Impact of Nightly Wine Drinking on Resting Heart Rate

## The Setup

Let's assume you're running a study to look at the effect of drinking a glass of wine each night on resting heart rate of a sample of healthy adult males. Unfortunately you forgot to check their resting heart rate before teh study, so you just have the post-study heart rates. This is a very clean A/B test design -- you have a control group and a treatment group, and you're just measuring their resting heart rates.

We're going to cook the books a bit so we can know the "True" underlying data generating process. This will allow us to assess how our model behaves, given that we know there is no effect. 

## The Data

To do this, we're going to assume the heart rates are all coming from the same underlying distribution. We're going to draw "subjects" from the same distribution for each group, and we're going to repeat this drawing process until we find a staitically significant p-value using a T-Test. The distribution we will use will have a mean resting heart rate is 60 bpm and a standard deviation of 5 bpm.

```{python}
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class SimulatedData:
    control: pd.Series = (None,)
    treated: pd.Series = (None,)
    df: pd.DataFrame = (None,)
    test_result: stats._stats_py.TtestResult = None


class DataSimulator:
    def __init__(self, distribution=stats.norm):
        self.distribution = distribution

    def simulate_null_data(
        self,
        mean=60,
        std=5,
        alpha=0.05,
        sample_size=10,
        return_significant=True,
        random_state=1,
    ):

        dist = self.distribution(loc=mean, scale=std)

        if return_significant:
            p_val = 1
            while p_val >= alpha:
                control = dist.rvs(size=sample_size, random_state=random_state)
                treated = dist.rvs(size=sample_size, random_state=random_state * 100)
                result = stats.ttest_ind(control, treated)
                p_val = result.pvalue
                random_state += 1
        else:
            control = dist.rvs(size=sample_size, random_state=random_state)
            treated = dist.rvs(size=sample_size, random_state=random_state * 100)
            result = stats.ttest_ind(control, treated)

        df = pd.DataFrame({"control": control, "treated": treated}).melt(
            var_name="condition", value_name="outcome"
        )

        data = SimulatedData(
            control=control, treated=treated, df=df, test_result=result
        )

        return data


simulator = DataSimulator()
data = simulator.simulate_null_data()
```

So it took us `{python}print(idx)` experiments to arrive at a significant result. Let's look at the data we got.

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(3, 5))

df = data.df.rename({"outcome": "heart_rate"}, axis=1).replace({"treated": "wine"})

df.pipe(
    (sns.swarmplot, "data"),
    x="condition",
    y="heart_rate",
    ax=ax,
    color="C1",
    s=7,
)

df.pipe(
    (sns.pointplot, "data"),
    x="condition",
    y="heart_rate",
    ax=ax,
)

# ax.set_ylim(50, 70)
```

Ok, so this shows a slight difference in resting heart rate due to wine drinking (though we know this is just spurrious because we designed it that way). But let's see if the Bayesian model can come to the rescue.

# Bayesian Approach with a Small Sample

## Weakly Informative Prior

We're going to use some generally informative priors about heart rate to set the stage here. We'll say the average resting heart rate is 60 with a standard deviation of 10 because we don't want to overly influence the result. We'll also assume an effect size of 0, but we'll give this prior a wide standard deviation ($\sigma=1$) because we don't want to cloude any effect that might be there. This is somewhat informative, but not very much. It just assumes a generally reasonable resting heart rate, and it assumes no effect, but the large sigma makes it pretty agnostic. It's going to let the data really drive the posterior where it wants to go. Let's see what the posterior looks like.

```{python}
import pymc as pm
import arviz as az

assumed_mean = df["heart_rate"].mean()
assumed_sigma = df["heart_rate"].std()

condition_idx, conditions = pd.factorize(df["condition"])

with pm.Model(coords={"condition": conditions}) as model:

    mu = pm.Normal("mu", mu=60, sigma=10)
    effect = pm.Normal("effect", mu=0, sigma=1)
    overall_sigma = pm.HalfNormal("sigma", sigma=5)

    treated_mu = pm.Deterministic("treated_mu", mu + (effect * overall_sigma))

    control_observed = pm.Normal(
        "control_observed",
        mu=mu,
        sigma=overall_sigma,
        observed=df.query("condition == 'control'")["heart_rate"],
    )
    treatment_observed = pm.Normal(
        "treatment_observed",
        mu=treated_mu,
        sigma=overall_sigma,
        observed=df.query("condition == 'wine'")["heart_rate"],
    )

with model:
    idata = pm.sample()

az.plot_trace(idata)
plt.tight_layout()
```

This shows good sampler convergence. And just eyeballing the wine effect, it looks like it will have the same issue as we had the with frequentist test -- high probability of increased heart rate due to wine. Let's look at it compared to what we saw for the frequentist version of the analysis.

```{python}
post_df = (
    idata.posterior[["mu", "treated_mu"]]
    .to_dataframe()
    .melt(var_name="condition", value_name="heart_rate")
    .replace({
        "mu": "control",
        "treated_mu": "wine"
    })
)

post_df["estimator"] = "mcmc"

fig, ax = plt.subplots()

df.pipe(
    (sns.swarmplot, "data"),
    x="condition",
    y="heart_rate",
    ax=ax,
    color="C1",
    s=7,
)

df.pipe(
    (sns.pointplot, "data"),
    x="condition",
    y="heart_rate",
    ax=ax,
    errorbar=("ci", 95),
    label="bootstrap"
)

post_df.pipe(
    (sns.pointplot, "data"),
    x="condition",
    y="heart_rate",
    ax=ax,
    errorbar=("pi", 95),
    color="C2",
    dodge=True,
    label="mcmc"
)
```

The Bayesian and Frequentist plots are pretty similar. There is some minor deviation, but not enough to change any inference.

Let's use a Bayesian Hypothesis Testing method, called the Bayes Factor. This is one of the ways people do inference using Bayesian posteriors. You compare the probability of a null value (i.e. 0) under the prior to the probability of the null value using the posterior. This tells you how much more or less likely the null value is now that you have observed data.

```{python}
result, ax = az.plot_bf(
    idata,
    var_name="effect",
    prior=stats.norm(loc=0, scale=1).rvs(size=10_000, random_state=100)
)
```

The Bayes Factor suggests the probability of the alternative (i.e. the Posterior) relative to the null (i.e. the prior) is `{python} result['BF10'].round(2)`, meaning the null is `{python} result['BF10'].round(2)`x more likely under the prior than under the posterior.

That's not thay much. Anything less than 3 is considered a small effect. But if you're making binary decisions, you would probably make a binary decision here.

However, you'll notice from the prior that our model allowed for an effect size in excess of 3 standard deviations. And it gives a fair amount of credibility to 1, or even 2 standard deviation changes in heart rate due to once-nightly wine consumption. This doesn't seem credible to me. Most effect sizes are very small, on the order of 0.2 standard deviations. 

## Informative Prior

So let's try this again, but with a different, more skeptical prior on the effect of wine. This time, we'll still assume the effect size is probably 0, but we'll change the prior so that $\sigma_{effect}=0.3$. Why 0.3? Because I looked at a distribution with this value, and thought it seemed about right for my own expectations (I wish I had a better justificaiton than "vibes," but I also think "vibes" should be an appropriate justification when you don't have anything else to go on).


```{python}
condition_idx, conditions = pd.factorize(df["condition"])

with pm.Model(coords={"condition": conditions}) as model:

    mu = pm.Normal("mu", mu=60, sigma=10)
    effect = pm.Normal("effect", mu=0, sigma=0.3)
    overall_sigma = pm.HalfNormal("sigma", sigma=5)

    treated_mu = pm.Deterministic("treated_mu", mu + (effect * overall_sigma))

    control_observed = pm.Normal(
        "control_observed",
        mu=mu,
        sigma=overall_sigma,
        observed=df.query("condition == 'control'")["heart_rate"],
    )
    treatment_observed = pm.Normal(
        "treatment_observed",
        mu=treated_mu,
        sigma=overall_sigma,
        observed=df.query("condition == 'wine'")["heart_rate"],
    )

with model:
    idata_skeptical = pm.sample()

result, ax = az.plot_bf(
    idata_skeptical,
    var_name="effect",
    prior=stats.norm(loc=0, scale=0.3).rvs(size=10_000, random_state=100)
)
```

Now the prior covers a more reasonable range. And the posterior is reduced a bit. The Bayes factor is quite small now, just `{python} result['BF10'].round(2)`, so this one is more of a toss-up. You would be hard-pressed to make a binary decision about it.

## Skeptical Prior

But let's say you're a very skeptical person. You really don't believe a glass of wine a night is going to impact your heart rate. To do this, we're just going to put an even stricter prior on the effect size. Since we're making the effect distribution based on vibes, there's no reason not to. So now let's make the effect size distribution $D ~ Normal(\mu=0, \sigma=0.1)$. That's pretty skeptical!

```{python}
condition_idx, conditions = pd.factorize(df["condition"])

with pm.Model(coords={"condition": conditions}) as model:

    mu = pm.Normal("mu", mu=60, sigma=10)
    effect = pm.Normal("effect", mu=0, sigma=0.1)
    overall_sigma = pm.HalfNormal("sigma", sigma=5)

    treated_mu = pm.Deterministic("treated_mu", mu + (effect * overall_sigma))

    control_observed = pm.Normal(
        "control_observed",
        mu=mu,
        sigma=overall_sigma,
        observed=df.query("condition == 'control'")["heart_rate"],
    )
    treatment_observed = pm.Normal(
        "treatment_observed",
        mu=treated_mu,
        sigma=overall_sigma,
        observed=df.query("condition == 'wine'")["heart_rate"],
    )

with model:
    idata_vskeptical = pm.sample()

result, ax = az.plot_bf(
    idata_vskeptical,
    var_name="effect",
    prior=stats.norm(loc=0, scale=0.1).rvs(size=10_000, random_state=100)
)
```

With the skeptical prior, the Bayes Factor is now `{python} result['BF10'].round(2)`. In other words, we really don't believe there's an effect. And that makes sense! There are only 10 observations per group! How could you possibly believe you've observed some super special significant effect with this few observations?

## Comparing Posteriors coming from Priors

Let's compare all the posteriors as a function of the priors now. This time, we'll ask what proportion of the posterior falls above and below 0. This will tell us the "probability of direction" of the observed effect.

```{python}
def plot_kde_with_threshold(data, threshold, ax, shade_alpha=0.3):
    
    # Plot KDE
    kde = sns.kdeplot(data, ax=ax, color="C0")
    
    # Get the KDE curve data
    line = kde.lines[0]
    x = line.get_xdata()
    y = line.get_ydata()
    
    # Find x range and indices where x is less than or equal to threshold
    idx_threshold = np.searchsorted(x, threshold)
    
    # Calculate area under the curve using numerical integration
    # Total area should be approximately 1 for a proper PDF
    total_area = np.trapz(y, x)
    
    # Area below threshold
    area_below = np.trapz(y[:idx_threshold], x[:idx_threshold]) / total_area
    # Area above threshold
    area_above = 1 - area_below
    
    # Shade the region below threshold
    ax.fill_between(x[:idx_threshold], y[:idx_threshold], alpha=shade_alpha, color="C1", 
                   label=f"Below: {area_below:.1%}")
    
    # Shade the region above threshold
    ax.fill_between(x[idx_threshold:], y[idx_threshold:], alpha=shade_alpha, color="C2", 
                   label=f"Above: {area_above:.1%}")
    
    # Add a vertical line at the threshold
    ax.axvline(x=threshold, color='black', linestyle='--', 
               label=f"Threshold: {threshold}")
    
    # Add percentage annotations in each region
    # Find positions for text
    below_x = np.mean(x[:idx_threshold]) if idx_threshold > 0 else min(x)
    below_y = np.max(y[:idx_threshold]) / 2 if idx_threshold > 0 else 0
    
    above_x = np.mean(x[idx_threshold:]) if idx_threshold < len(x) else max(x)
    above_y = np.max(y[idx_threshold:]) / 2 if idx_threshold < len(x) else 0
    
    # Add text annotations
    ax.text(below_x, below_y, f"{area_below:.1%}", 
            ha='center', va='center', color='black', fontweight='bold')
    ax.text(above_x, above_y, f"{area_above:.1%}", 
            ha='center', va='center', color='black', fontweight='bold')
    
    # Add legend
    ax.legend()
    
    return ax

fig, axs = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(4, 7), sharex=True)

for inference, ax, title in zip([idata, idata_skeptical, idata_vskeptical], axs, ["Weakly Informative", "Informative", "Skeptical"]):

    posterior = inference.posterior.effect.data.flatten()
    plot_kde_with_threshold(posterior, 0.0, ax)
    ax.set_title(title)
```

This is a really important plot. It shows us that when we assume basically nothing, we can very easily conclude that there's a high probability that wine lowers resting heart rate. When we add a slightly more stringent prior, this reduces, but does not eliminate this issue. Finally, when we enforce a very strict prior because we are pretty confident a small amount of wine shouldn't have a massive impact on resting heart rate, we find that we really aren't sure.

In this case, because we were only using 10 atheletes in each group, we would say that "the data is overwhelmed by the prior." In other words, when we use an informative prior, we find that the amount of data we have just isn't enough to convince us that wine matters. 

But does this hold up when we have more data? What if we have 100 people in each group?

# Bayesian Approach with a Larger Sample

We're going to use the same procedure here as we used previously -- we'll draw 100 control and 100 treated samples from the same distribution over and over until we have a stistically significant difference using a Frequentist approach.

```{python}
data = simulator.simulate_null_data(sample_size=100)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(3, 5))

df = data.df.rename({"outcome": "heart_rate"}, axis=1).replace({"treated": "wine"})

df.pipe(
    (sns.swarmplot, "data"),
    x="condition",
    y="heart_rate",
    ax=ax,
    color="C1",
    s=7,
)

df.pipe(
    (sns.pointplot, "data"),
    x="condition",
    y="heart_rate",
    ax=ax,
)
```

There are a lot more observations now. This should bring some precision to our estimates!

```{python}
condition_idx, conditions = pd.factorize(df["condition"])

with pm.Model(coords={"condition": conditions}) as model:

    mu = pm.Normal("mu", mu=60, sigma=10)
    effect = pm.Normal("effect", mu=0, sigma=1)
    overall_sigma = pm.HalfNormal("sigma", sigma=5)

    treated_mu = pm.Deterministic("treated_mu", mu + (effect * overall_sigma))

    control_observed = pm.Normal(
        "control_observed",
        mu=mu,
        sigma=overall_sigma,
        observed=df.query("condition == 'control'")["heart_rate"],
    )
    treatment_observed = pm.Normal(
        "treatment_observed",
        mu=treated_mu,
        sigma=overall_sigma,
        observed=df.query("condition == 'wine'")["heart_rate"],
    )

    idata = pm.sample()

with pm.Model(coords={"condition": conditions}) as model:

    mu = pm.Normal("mu", mu=60, sigma=10)
    effect = pm.Normal("effect", mu=0, sigma=0.3)
    overall_sigma = pm.HalfNormal("sigma", sigma=5)

    treated_mu = pm.Deterministic("treated_mu", mu + (effect * overall_sigma))

    control_observed = pm.Normal(
        "control_observed",
        mu=mu,
        sigma=overall_sigma,
        observed=df.query("condition == 'control'")["heart_rate"],
    )
    treatment_observed = pm.Normal(
        "treatment_observed",
        mu=treated_mu,
        sigma=overall_sigma,
        observed=df.query("condition == 'wine'")["heart_rate"],
    )

    idata_skeptical = pm.sample()

with pm.Model(coords={"condition": conditions}) as model:

    mu = pm.Normal("mu", mu=60, sigma=10)
    effect = pm.Normal("effect", mu=0, sigma=0.1)
    overall_sigma = pm.HalfNormal("sigma", sigma=5)

    treated_mu = pm.Deterministic("treated_mu", mu + (effect * overall_sigma))

    control_observed = pm.Normal(
        "control_observed",
        mu=mu,
        sigma=overall_sigma,
        observed=df.query("condition == 'control'")["heart_rate"],
    )
    treatment_observed = pm.Normal(
        "treatment_observed",
        mu=treated_mu,
        sigma=overall_sigma,
        observed=df.query("condition == 'wine'")["heart_rate"],
    )

    idata_vskeptical = pm.sample()
```

## Assessing Prior Differences

```{python}
fig, axs = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(4, 7), sharex=True)

for inference, ax, title in zip([idata, idata_skeptical, idata_vskeptical], axs, ["Weakly Informative", "Informative", "Skeptical"]):

    posterior = inference.posterior.effect.data.flatten()
    plot_kde_with_threshold(posterior, 0.0, ax)
    ax.set_title(title)
```

So we can see here that even with the skeptical prior, when you have 100 observations per group you still become pretty convinced there's a difference, even when we know it's just spurrious.

But this brings us to another advantage of the Bayesian approach -- we can ask the question "What's the probability that the effect is _meaningful_." And we get to define what meaningful is. And let's say that anything less than a -0.2 standard devitaion reduction, we just don't care about.

## Assessing "Meaningfullness"

```{python}
fig, axs = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(4, 7), sharex=True)

for inference, ax, title in zip([idata, idata_skeptical, idata_vskeptical], axs, ["Weakly Informative", "Informative", "Skeptical"]):

    posterior = inference.posterior.effect.data.flatten()
    plot_kde_with_threshold(posterior, -0.2, ax)
    ax.set_title(title)
```

So now a skeptic will believe it's unlikely to have a meaningful impact. Someone who's willing to give the benefit of the doubt will believe that it probably matters, but there's a decent chance it really doesn't. And someone who knows basically nothing going into it is still only 77% sure that the effect matters at all.

I can hear so many past colleagues saying to me "this is way too confusing -- does it have an effect or doesn't it?" This is fundamentally where my perspective differs. The goal is not to ask "True/False, is there something here or not?" Instead, the goal is to say "To what degree do I believe something is happening in light of what I believed before, and what I have observed?" 

This is the real strength of Bayesian reasoning. With traditional null hypothesis significance testing, you're forced to ask a stilly question with a binary answer. With Bayesian methods you're able to ask the questions you actually care about, and quantify the degree to which you believe values are plausible.
